questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =5x,$ we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡10x={cos}^{2}⁡5x-{sin}^{2}⁡5x.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (3{x}^{2}+10{sin}^{2}⁡5x-10{cos}^{2}⁡5x)\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}-10({cos}^{2}⁡5x-{sin}^{2}⁡5x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3{x}^{2}-10\operatorname{cos}⁡10x)\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}-10(\frac{1}{10}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡10x)+C \\  & ={x}^{3}-\operatorname{sin}⁡10x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Cosine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =2x$, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡2x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5-8{cos}^{2}⁡2x)\text{d}x & =\int [5-8\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & =\int [5-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & =\int (1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x)\text{d}x \\  & =x-4(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+C \\  & =x-\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Sine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)={sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+C \\  & =\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Sine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
questions.worked_solution:
Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,$ so letting $\theta =3x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)-4{sin}^{2}⁡(3x) & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)-4{sin}^{2}⁡(3x) \\  & =1-5{sin}^{2}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =3x,$ we have

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x))={sin}^{2}⁡(3x).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(1-5{sin}^{2}⁡(3x))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(1-5\cdot \frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)-\frac{3}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{5}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)-\frac{3}{2}x)\,|}_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3} \\  & =[\frac{5}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{5\pi }{3})-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{5\pi }{3}]-[\frac{5}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}] \\  & =[0-\frac{5\pi }{2}]-[0-\frac{\pi }{2}] \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069587/assets/e0a3fb0f4fc900f6ef8ac041ded7553f7ac44cc09f946bc3ebfee8a3235e8e94.png)

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=5{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+1,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=0,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(5{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+1)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1,$ so we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}5{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+1 & =3{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2({sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{cos}^{2}⁡(2x))+1 \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1.
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(3{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(\frac{3}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\frac{9}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{3}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\frac{9}{2}x)\,|}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =(\frac{3}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡0+\frac{9}{2}\cdot 0)-(\frac{3}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )+\frac{9}{2}\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =(0+0)-(0-\frac{9\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
